title: multinomialProb: PMF Definition and Nonnegativity
content: `multinomialProb s p n k` defines the probability mass function of the multinomial distribution: $\binom{n}{k} \prod_{i \in s} p(i)^{k(i)}$ where $\binom{n}{k} = \text{Nat.multinomial}\, s\, k$ is the multinomial coefficient. The function is parameterized by a finite set $s$, probability function $p : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$, number of trials $n$, and outcome function $k : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$. `multinomialProb_nonneg` proves nonnegativity when all $p(i) \geq 0$ via `mul_nonneg`: the multinomial coefficient casts to $\geq 0$, and the product of powers of nonneg numbers is nonneg.
mathContext: The multinomial coefficient $\binom{n}{k_1,\ldots,k_m} = \frac{n!}{k_1! \cdots k_m!}$ counts the number of ways to assign $n$ distinguishable trials to $m$ outcome categories with $k_i$ trials in category $i$. In Lean, `Nat.multinomial s k` with `∑ i ∈ s, k i = n` gives this coefficient. The `piAntidiag s n` finset contains exactly the functions $k : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ with support in $s$ and $\sum k(i) = n$ — the valid outcome distributions.

title: multinomialProb_sum_eq_one: Normalization IS the Multinomial Theorem
content: `multinomialProb_sum_eq_one` proves $\sum_{k : \sum k = n} P(k) = 1$ in 3 lines: unfold the definition, apply `Finset.sum_pow_eq_sum_piAntidiag` (the multinomial theorem), then rewrite using $\sum p(i) = 1$ to get $1^n = 1$. The proof is: `rw [hp, one_pow] at h; exact h.symm`. The multinomial theorem literally *is* the normalization proof — no further work needed.
mathContext: The multinomial theorem states $(\sum_{i \in s} x_i)^n = \sum_{k \in \text{piAntidiag}\, s\, n} \binom{n}{k} \prod_{i \in s} x_i^{k(i)}$. Setting $x_i = p(i)$ and using $\sum p(i) = 1$: the left side becomes $1^n = 1$. The right side is $\sum_{k} \text{multinomialProb}\, s\, p\, n\, k$. This identifies probability normalization with the multinomial theorem, showing probability theory and combinatorics are two faces of the same algebraic identity.

title: MGF Derivation: multinomial_weighted_sum and multinomial_mgf_factored
content: `multinomial_weighted_sum` proves $(\sum p(i) \cdot g(i))^n = \sum_{k} \binom{n}{k} \prod (p(i) g(i))^{k(i)}$ — again a direct application of `sum_pow_eq_sum_piAntidiag` with $f(i) = p(i) \cdot g(i)$. `multinomial_mgf_factored` then factors $(p(i) g(i))^{k(i)} = p(i)^{k(i)} \cdot g(i)^{k(i)}$ using `Finset.prod_mul_distrib` and `mul_pow`, separating probability weights from the $g$-terms. This works over *any commutative semiring* — not just $\mathbb{R}$.
mathContext: The generality is key: the MGF derivation holds in any `CommSemiring`, so it applies to formal power series (generating functions), polynomial rings, and more. The factorization $\prod (p \cdot g)^k = (\prod p^k)(\prod g^k)$ is the multiplicativity of the product over independent factors, proved by `Finset.prod_mul_distrib`. When $g(i) = \exp(t_i)$: $\sum P(k) \prod g(i)^{k(i)} = \mathbb{E}[\exp(\sum t_i X_i)] = (\sum p(i) e^{t_i})^n$, the classical MGF formula.

title: Binomial as 2-Outcome Multinomial: Bool-Indexed Distribution
content: `multinomial_is_binomial` proves that the multinomial distribution over `{false, true}` with $p(\text{true}) = p$, $p(\text{false}) = 1-p$ normalizes to 1. The proof calls `multinomialProb_sum_eq_one` after reducing $\sum_{b \in \{F,T\}} p(b) = (1-p) + p = 1$ via `ring`. `binomial_normalization` proves the same result directly: $((1-p) + p)^n = 1^n = 1$ by `simp`.
mathContext: For $s = \{F, T\}$, `piAntidiag {F,T} n` contains functions $k : \text{Bool} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $k(F) + k(T) = n$, corresponding to $(n-j, j)$ for $j = 0, \ldots, n$. The multinomial coefficient $\binom{n}{n-j, j} = \binom{n}{j}$ is the standard binomial coefficient. So $P(k) = \binom{n}{j} p^j (1-p)^{n-j}$ — exactly the binomial PMF. This shows `binomial-theorem-oq-03` (binomial distribution) is a special case derivable from this more general formalization.

title: multinomial_count: |s|^n = ∑ Multinomial Coefficients
content: `multinomial_count` proves $|s|^n = \sum_{k \in \text{piAntidiag}\, s\, n} \binom{n}{k}$ by applying `sum_pow_eq_sum_piAntidiag` with $f \equiv 1$: $(\sum_{i \in s} 1)^n = (|s|)^n$ and $\prod_{i \in s} 1^{k(i)} = 1$. This is the multinomial analog of $\sum_{j=0}^n \binom{n}{j} = 2^n$. For $|s| = 2$: the identity says $2^n = \sum_{j=0}^n \binom{n}{j}$ (sum of binomial coefficients). The proof uses `simp` with `one_pow`, `prod_const_one`, `sum_const`, and cast lemmas.
mathContext: The identity $|s|^n = \sum_{k} \binom{n}{k}$ counts two things: $|s|^n$ is the number of functions $\text{Fin}\, n \to s$ (all sequences of $n$ choices from $s$); $\sum_k \binom{n}{k}$ counts by distributing $n$ trials into outcome categories. The bijection is: any function $f : \text{Fin}\, n \to s$ induces an outcome count $k(i) = |f^{-1}(\{i\})|$, and $\binom{n}{k}$ counts the functions with that distribution. This is the counting argument underlying both the multinomial theorem and the multinomial distribution.
